text:
Interviewer: Could you tell me your name please, and where you were from.
Interviewee: The name from now, or the name from — from Koretz?
Interviewer: Let’s do both.
Interviewee: Huh?
Interviewer: Your name in Koretz.
Interviewee: In Koretz. You spell it P-e-t-e-y, Petey Miller, M-i-l-l-e-r, that’s in Polish.
Interviewer: And in English?
Interviewee: In English, P-e-t-e, Pete, M-i-l-l-e-r.
Interviewer: And you’re from Koretz?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Can you tell me a little bit about Koretz that you remember before the war?
Interviewee: Yes. Come from a very small town, very happy town, not too many people. Nobody left over there right now, but we were there and we were very happy. We didn't have nothing, but was hap — we were happy.
Interviewer: How many Jews were in the town, do you know?
Interviewee: I would say about 3,000.
Interviewer: 3,000. And how large was this — was the town?
Interviewee: Huh?
Interviewer: How large was the town, total?
Interviewee: Altogether, including the Polish people and everything else, probably about six.
Interviewer: So 50 percent you think, were Jews.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: And how large was your family?
Interviewee: How large?
Interviewer: Your family.
Interviewee: Yeah. I have a — a brother and two sisters.
Interviewer: And what are their name — what were their names?
Interviewee: Their name, my f — my brothers — my fir-first name, Emma, the sister, my older sister. My brother was Matej, and my younger sister were Alice.
Interviewer: And your parent’s name? Your parent’s names?
Interviewee: Mash, my father, and Evalyne is my mother.
Interviewer: And aunts and uncles, cousins?
Interviewee: Yes, we have uncles over there. Used to be, but not there any more.
Interviewer: How large do you think the family was?
Interviewee: The family was about 25 people, in different dir — different places there.
Interviewer: But all near Koretz?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: And — and how many survived the war?
Interviewee: Survivor was myself, and my sister. Three.
Interviewer: Three. Did you come from a religious family?
Interviewee: Well, in between.
Interviewer: Mo-Modern Orthodox?
Interviewee: Yeah, yeah.
Interviewer: Yeah. So your father didn’t have a beard and pay — pay —
Interviewee: No, no, no.
Interviewer: Well, what was a — what was a Friday night like in — at your house?
Interviewee: On a Friday night we *** together, on a Saturday, we ha — have been to s-synagogue, all the time.
Interviewer: And do you remember any holidays that —
Interviewee: ***
Interviewer: — Pesach? ***
Interviewee: Oh yeah, oh yeah, big.
Interviewer: So you would have —
Interviewee: My mother was a real good cook, and she made a — she would — there’s a lot of people all the time.
Interviewer: What did your father do?
Interviewee: My father was — was in the cattle business.
Interviewer: So he had non-Jewish customers?
Interviewee: Ah, what?
Interviewer: He had non-Jewish customers?
Interviewee: Oh, a lot of them, yeah.
Interviewer: And w-was there ever any trouble with — with them?
Interviewee: With them? No. We had gotten along very good til the end. On the end we have a fellow that he was my brother’s best friend for 22 years. And when the Germans came in, he became a policeman. And he is the one — the first one that came into the house and liked my mother very much, and walked into the house as — dressed up as a policeman, he says, open up the closets over here. She opened the closet and he takes out a — a suit that my brother used to wear, and he put on the suit, how’d it fit me, it’s okay, then took the coat, it’s okay. Then took my brother and killed my brother.
Interviewer: He killed your brother?
Interviewee: Yeah. *** His — my next door neighbor, the best friend ran away. He was doing it to a lot of people. *** us, we were very shocked at that time, the family. So after the war, my sister was on the underground. She had about 500 people working for her. She came back to town, to mine town, to my Koretz, she became the mayor on that time. As she was going out to Kiev, she was there in the Kiev and a lot of people come in to the place to make out passport to go away someplace else. As she walks in, in the hallway she sees a lot of people sitting. And she sees the guy what killed my brother sitting over there. She walks into the mayor, says, what’s the guy’s name? So the guy comes in, what’s your name? Max Maximilian. That’s *** name. And my mother — my sister, sitting there, she says, you are lying. You are Prisha Baumann. You killed my brother. He starts shaking. And right away they got a police, put some handcuffs on him, they arrested him, and they brought him back to my town, to Koretz. He came into Koretz, was a lot of *** where they came back from the army sa — one without a leg, one without a arm, and everybody knows what he was doing to the Jews over there, he was in jail. They brought in his wife, his wife was standing right there, says, well, what would you do for him? She says, kill him. She says, I begged him not to do it. You people were our friends, you know, and he done some things. Ev-Everybody started doing something to him. This one put a knife, this one punched him, this and that make — in the long run, they made sure he killed — is killed *** it’s not an easy thing to talk about it, but *** yeah.
Interviewer: You went to school in Koretz?
Interviewee: Where?
Interviewer: You went to school?
Interviewee: Me?
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: Was it a public school?
Interviewee: I’m — yes.
Interviewer: So it wasn’t a — it wasn’t a cheder?
Interviewee: No, I was — I go in both, I was *** Hebrew school, even was going there, and I was going a public school, Polish.
Interviewer: So what would — what would a typical day be like for you when you were young, when you were a child?
Interviewee: That — the — the name?
Interviewer: What would a — what would a typical day be? How would you — you get up in the morning and what would you do?
Interviewee: What I was doing when I got up in the morning? When I was younger *** take me to go to school, yeah.
Interviewer: And then when would you go to cheder?
Interviewee: The cheder, going for about an hour, an hour and a half. Then I used to have a tutor come into the house, too.
Interviewer: So this is after school?
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: And you had a tutor, so he would ask you questions of —
Interviewee: Oh yeah.
Interviewer: Were you Bar Mitzvahed?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Do you remember when the Russians came in?
Interviewee: 1939.
Interviewer: Where were you then?
Interviewee: In Koretz.
Interviewer: You — you were living in Koretz?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: What was that like when the Russians came?
Interviewee: It was no ***. They walked in, we were just a mile away from the — from the border. So they walked in, was no shooting, no nothing, they just came in and everybody was happy. They made us — made us happy, you know. So, pretend like it — nothing happened, in the first couple days.
Interviewer: But then what?
Interviewee: Then start up more to find out that’s not — not so good. So being over there, the first thing they drove in over there was cars, and I was *** bike, driving my bike, and the guy comes up to me, would you like to sell me the bike? I said I don’t want to sell the bike. I bought a bike, cost me t — 10 dollars. ***. Then they walked in with the rubles and they said to me, sell me this. I said, I don’t want to sell it. So he takes out and shows me he’s gonna give me 150 for it — for the bike.
Interviewer: Rubles?
Interviewee: Yeah. Rubles, but I didn’t know what a ruble is worth. So I sold it for 150. I came back and show it to my father, I got 150 dollars. He says, that’s a lot of money, maybe the money’s worth nothing, he says. So I got scared, so I went out to bought a couple other bikes, and I paid 10 - 12 dollars, and I ride back and start selling them ***. Some I sell for 150, some 200, you know *** money, I could see the money is nothing, but shows pretty good like I’m a — a big man already, I got five - 600 dollars.
Interviewer: And you were how old at this time?
Interviewee: Pardon?
Interviewer: How old were you?
Interviewee: 16.
Interviewer: Di — had you heard of Hitler before?
Interviewee: Hm?
Interviewer: Had you heard of Hitler? Did you know what was happening in Germany?
Interviewee: At that time, was nothing, was just started up. No, I didn't know. I know *** the papers about anti-Semitism’s going on, everything else, but not — not for sure because we were very out of it.
Interviewer: But you — and the war had started. What did you think when the war started?
Interviewee: What I think? I didn't like it, but it was there, the war.
Interviewer: Did you think it would come to — to Koretz?
Interviewee: To go back to Koretz?
Interviewer: Did — did you think the war would reach Koretz?
Interviewee: *** the war?
Interviewer: Well, the war started and they invaded Poland.
Interviewee: Yes, that’s the course, they invaded right — I — I was Poland, I was there.
Interviewer: But you were — but you were a Soviet. You were a Russian.
Interviewee: That’s Russia, the Russia, yeah, that’s where the Russians came in, yes.
